Iridium-Catalyzed Enantioselective Formal meta-Allenylation of
Pyridines
Pankaj Roy+, Pratibha Mahto +, and Santanu Mukherjee*
Abstract: Site-selective functionalization of pyridines is an important yet challenging transformation. T emporary
dearomatization of pyridines through redox-neutral cycloaddition has recently emerged as a reliable and attractive strategy
for meta-functionalization of pyridines. Despite the amenability of the resulting bench-stable cycloadduct, oxazinopyridine,
to a variety of electrophilic and radical-based reagents, its enantioselective functionalization remains unexplored. Herein,
we present the ﬁrst enantioselective meta-functionalization of pyridines through the intermediacy of oxazinopyridines. This
highly enantioselective formal meta-allenylation of pyridines is achieved by treating the easily accessible oxazinopyridines
with racemic allenylic alcohol under the combination of a catalytic amount of an Ir(I)/(P , oleﬁn) complex and Lewis
acidic Sc(OTf)3 followed by acid-mediated rearomatization. With oxazinopyridines derived from unsubstituted or suitably
substituted pyridines, iterative 3,5-difunctionalization is possible, which also allows for the stereodivergent synthesis of all
four stereoisomers of 3,5-bis-allenylic pyridines.
Introduction
Pyridine is among the most abundant nitrogenous het-
erocycles in natural products, [1] pharmaceuticals,[2–4] and
agrochemicals[5] (Figure 1). Pyridine derivatives also serve
as ligands[6] and catalysts[7,8] in asymmetric synthesis besides
acting as precursors to targets of biological and material
importance.[9] Consequently, site-selective functionalization
of pyridines is a highly sought-after transformation. Direct
C–H functionalization is the most straightforward avenue
of decorating pyridines. [10,11] The inherent electron-deﬁcient
nature of pyridines renders their ortho- and para-positions
electrophilic and amenable to nucleophilic substitution
(Scheme 1a).[12,13] In contrast, meta-functionalization of
pyridines is challenging. [14–16] Electrophilic aromatic substi-
tution reactions such as nitration [17] and bromination [18] of
pyridines are known but require harsh reaction conditions,
which restrict their application.
The adversities associated with functionalizing the meta-
position of pyridines have spurred innovative strategies
in recent years. [14,15] V arious approaches, including
directing group-assisted C–H activation, [19,20] non-directed
metalation,[21–23] and temporary dearomatization of the
pyridine ring, [24,25] have been explored to enable meta-
functionalization, of which the latter emerged as the most
attractive one (Scheme 1b). Among different temporary
dearomatization strategies adopted so far, [24,26–31] the redox-

neutral dearomatization of pyridine through cycloaddition is
particularly noteworthy.
In 1967, Huisgen et al. reported a three-component
cycloaddition of pyridine or isoquinoline with dimethyl
acetylenedicarboxylate (DMAD) and phenyl isocyanate,
which could be converted back to its components upon
heating.[32] The Nair group further advanced this area by
substituting phenyl isocyanate with other dipolarophiles,
thereby expanding the scope of this reaction. [33–36]
Notwithstanding the reversibility of this cycloaddition
reaction, its potential in functionalizing pyridines was not
realized until recently. In 2022, Studer et al. exploited
this strategy to transform pyridines into bench-stable
dearomatized oxazinopyridines C, via Huisgen 1,4-
dipolar cycloaddition with DMAD and methyl pyruvate
(Scheme 1b).[28] These oxazinopyridines (oxazinoazines)
are nucleophilic in nature by virtue of their (di)enamine
character and may be viewed as meta-nucleophilic pyridine
surrogates. Consequently, they have been intercepted with a
variety of electrophiles and radical-based reagents prior to
rearomatization to afford meta-substituted pyridines. [28,37–41]
In addition, meta-sulfonylation of pyridines has also been
achieved under electrochemical [42] or photochemical
conditions.[43,44]
Despite their growing popularity, the application of these
meta-nucleophilic pyridine surrogates in catalytic transforma-
tions is rare. [40,43] Moreover, this redox-neutral dearomati-
zation strategy has never been applied for enantioselective
functionalization of pyridines or any other azines. In fact,
the only examples of enantioselective meta-functionalization
of pyridines, reported by Wang et al., involve reductive
dearomatization of pyridines. [45,46] These processes comprise
of borane-catalyzed dearomative hydroboration of pyridines
to 1,4-dihydropyridines ( A,S c h e m e 1b) followed by Pd-
or Ir-catalyzed enantioselective meta-allylation and oxidative
rearomatization.

In an effort to expand the synthetic toolbox for enan-
tioselective functionalization of pyridines with precise meta-
regioselectivity, we herein report the ﬁrst enantioselective
functionalization of oxazinopyridines en route to chiral meta-
functionalized pyridines.[47]
As a part of our research program on enantioselec-
tive C(sp 2)–H allenylation under iridium catalysis, [48,49] we
became interested in introducing an allenylic substituent at
the meta-position of pyridines. Ir-catalyzed allenylic sub-
stitution reaction was ﬁrst reported by T akeuchi et al.
in 2004. [50] However, Ir-catalyzed enantioselective allenylic
substitution was pioneered by the Carreira group and was
proposed to proceed via an Ir-bound allenylic carbocation
intermediate.[51–53] Recent studies by our laboratory [48] and
the T akeuchi group[54] demonstrated the utility of this catalyst
system for Friedel–Crafts allenylation of (hetero)arenes.
However, electron-deﬁcient nature of pyridines precludes
their direct application in Friedel–Crafts allenylation.
We hypothesized that the nucleophilic (di)enamine func-
tionality of oxazinopyridines [28] can be intercepted with an
Ir-bound electrophilic allenylic fragment [53] (Scheme 1c).
Subsequent acid-mediated rearomatization would furnish
chiral pyridine derivatives, bearing a synthetically versatile
allenylic group at the meta-position.
ResultsandDiscussion
We embarked upon testing our hypothesis by selecting
oxazinopyridine 2a, derived through dearomatization of

pyridine ( 1a), as the model substrate (Scheme 2a).[28] Both
C3 and C5 positions of 2a are nucleophilic owing to their
dienamine and enamine reactivity, respectively, which gives
rise to the possibility of over-allenylation. Therefore, it
was imperative to identify conditions for selective mono-
allenylation of 2a at the outset of our investigation. The Ir(I)-
complex derived in situ from a 1:2 mixture of [Ir(COD)Cl] 2
and Carreira’s ( P, oleﬁn) ligand [55] (Sa)-L was selected as
the catalyst candidate. A reaction of 2a with an excess (1.7
equiv) of racemic allenylic alcohol 3a, in the presence of
6 mol% of the Ir(I)/( Sa)-L complex and 10 mol% of Sc(OTf) 3
at 70 °C, indeed furnished bis-allenylic oxazinopyridine 4aa′
predominantly in an overall 58% yield within 21 h. The exact
position of the allenylic substituent in 4aa (i.e., C3 or C5),
although inconsequential for the ﬁnal outcome, could not be
determined. T reatment of this mixture of 4aa and 4aa′ with
2 M HCl in acetonitrile at 60 °C led to rearomatization and
afforded a 1:5 mixture of 3-allenylic pyridine ( 5aa)a n d3 ,
5-bis-allenylic pyridine ( 5aa′) in 90% yield essentially as a
single enantiomer for each of them (Scheme 2a,e n t r y1 ) .
Lowering the temperature to 45 °C in an attempt to prevent
over-allenylation proved futile, as 5aa′ still formed as the
major product (Scheme 2a, entry 2). However, reversing
the stoichiometry of 2a and 3a reduced the extent of bis-
allenylation considerably. Finally, a 3:1 ratio of 2a and 3a
turned out to be the optimum and favored mono-allenylation
(5aa/5aa′15:1). Under these conditions, 5aa was isolated in an
overall 36% yield with >99:1 e.r. (Scheme 2a,e n t r y4 ) .
Starting with these initial conditions for selective mono-
allenylation of 2a en route to meta-allenylic pyridine 5aa,
we undertook a detailed optimization of various reaction
parameters for improving the yield of 5aa (see Supporting
Information). These variables included promoter, reaction
medium, temperature, and initial concentration for the alleny-
lation step as well as the choice of acid and temperature for
the rearomatization step.
These studies revealed a combination of 6 mol% of the
Ir(I)/(Sa)-L complex and 20 mol% of Sc(OTf) 3 to be the
optimum for the allenylation reaction at 70 °C in THF
(Scheme 2b). Subsequent rearomatization with 4 M HCl in
acetonitrile at 60 °C afforded meta-allenylic pyridine 5aa with
>99.5:0.5 e.r. in 65% yield over two steps. It is worth noting
that oxazinopyridine 2a contains two stereocenters and forms
as an inseparable mixture of diastereomers (with 4.5:1 d.r.).
However, the stereochemistry of 2a did not seem to have
any effect on the ﬁnal stereochemical outcome, since 5aa
was isolated with outstanding e.r. The enantioinduction of
the allenylation reaction was completely controlled by the
Ir(I)/(Sa)-L complex.
Similarly, 3-substituted pyridines can give rise to two
regioisomeric oxazinopyridines, which are inseparable. How-
ever, each of these oxazinopyridines contains only one
accessible position for allenylation and upon rearomatization
should converge into the same product. As expected from the
reaction with 2a, catalyst controlled-enantioinduction should
override the substrate control. Indeed, when oxazinopyridine
2b, derived from 3-methyl pyridine 1b, was reacted as a
mixture of diastereo- and regioisomers in a 1:1.2 ratio with
rac-3a, the 3-allenylic 5-methyl pyridine 5ba was isolated
in 68% yield with >99.5:0.5 e.r. (Scheme 2b). Clearly, each
isomer of 2b yields the same product enantiomer upon
rearomatization with equally high enantioselectivity.
Having optimized the reaction conditions, the scope and
limitations of meta-allenylation of pyridines were investi-
gated. We ﬁrst sought to examine the scope of pyridines
in this reaction (Scheme 3). A variety of oxazinopyridines
(2b-q), derived from 3-substituted pyridines, reacted efﬁ-
ciently with allenylic alcohol rac-3a under our optimized
reaction conditions. In all these cases, the isomeric mixtures
of oxazinopyridines were employed as substrate, and the
corresponding meta-allenylic pyridines 5ba-qa were obtained
in moderate to good yields over two steps with uniformly
outstanding e.r. Electron-rich oxazinopyridines ( 2b-h) turned
out to be superior substrates compared to most of the
electron-deﬁcient ones ( 2i-q), as the products with relatively
higher yields were generally observed with the former.
Protected functionalities on oxazinopyridines such as NHBoc
(2e), OAc ( 2g), acetal ( 2l) didn’t hamper the allenylation
reaction, but the protecting groups fell off under the acidic
conditions employed for the rearomatization step. However,
we were pleased to note that other functional groups such as
amide and ketone survived all three steps.

In the case of 2-substituted pyridines, availability of both
3- and 5-positions gives rise to the possibility of regioiso-
meric allenylation apart from bis-allenylation. Interestingly,
oxazinopyridine 2r, derived from 2-phenyl pyridine, did
not pose any regioselectivity issue and furnished 2-phenyl
5-allenylic pyridine 5ra exclusively with excellent enantios-
electivity, albeit in only 32% yield. The same trend was
observed with other 2-aryl pyridine-derived oxazinopyridines
(2s-u). In these instances, allenylation proceeded through
the dienamine functionality of the oxazinopyridine to avoid
steric repulsion with the aryl substituent. T o the best of our
knowledge, this is the ﬁrst example of enantioselective C5-
functionalization of 2-aryl pyridines. Unfortunately, 2-alkyl
pyridines failed to react in the Huisgen 1,4-dipolar cycloaddi-
tion step to generate oxazinopyridines and, therefore, aren’t
compatible with this dearomative meta-allenylation strategy.
2-Heteroaryl pyridines furnished the desired product but in
low yield (see Supporting Information).
4-Methyl pyridine-derived oxazinopyridine 2v is also
amenable to allenylation under our optimized reaction con-
ditions and led only to mono-allenylation: The 3-allenylic
4-methyl pyridine 5va was isolated in moderate yield with
high enantiopurity. 5,6,7,8-T etrahydroisoquinoline ( 1w)v i a
dearomative meta-allenylation gave access to polysubstituted
pyridine 5wa in decent yield.
Subsequently, we became interested in exploring other
structurally related azines, such as quinoline, isoquinoline,
etc., under our protocol. While the dearomatized interme-
diate derived from quinoline did not participate in the
allenylation reaction, isoquinoline ( 1x) smoothly produced
4-allenylic isoquinoline 5xa in 37% yield with 95.5:4.5 e.r.
After showcasing the scope of azines, we turned to
explore the scope of allenylic alcohols (Scheme 4). For this
purpose, oxazinopyridine 2b, derived from 3-methyl pyridine
(1b), was selected as the nucleophile. An array of electron-
rich (3b-d) and electron-deﬁcient ( 3e-g) para-substituted aryl
allenylic alcohols underwent successful substitution reaction
with 3-methyl oxazinopyridine ( 2b) and delivered the 3-
allenylic 5-methyl pyridines ( 5bb-bg) in moderate to good
yields with uniformly high enantioselectivity. In addition,

Given the prevalence of multifunctional heterocycles in
bioactive molecules, [2–4] systematic installation of function-
alities around the pyridine core in a site-selective manner
is an alluring goal. However, such a transformation, espe-
cially involving an enantioselective step, is elusive. Exclusive
C3-selective allenylation of 6-phenyl oxazinopyridine ( 2r)
intrigued us to assess the possibility of introducing a less
sterically demanding electrophile adjacent to the phenyl
group following enantioselective allenylation. Accordingly,
when 3-allenylic 6-phenyl oxazinopyridine 4ra was subjected
to a reaction with N-chlorosuccinimide (NCS) in CH 2Cl2
at 70 °C, [28] chlorination through the enamine functionality
of 4ra indeed took place to yield 5-allenylic-3-chloro-2-
phenylpyridine 10 after rearomatization (Scheme 6).
During the optimization studies (Scheme 2a), bis-
allenylation was encountered with unsubstituted oxazinopy-
ridine 2a. Using 2.2 equiv of rac-3a in this reaction, C2-
symmetric 3,5-bis-allenylic pyridine 5aa′ was isolated with
excellent relative ( >20:1 d.r.) and absolute ( >99.5:0.5 e.r.)
stereocontrol (Scheme 7a). The absence of meso-product
indicates complete ligand control in the second allenylation
and opens avenues for stereodivergent [57] iterative bis-
allenylation of pyridine with two different allenylic alcohols.
T o achieve this goal, controlled mono-allenylation was
performed using an excess of oxazinopyridine 2a for the reac-
tion with 4-ﬂuorophenyl allenylic alcohol rac-3f (Scheme 7b).
Under our otherwise standard reaction conditions, both
stereoisomers of 4af were isolated in good yield. The second
allenylation of 4af with 2-naphthyl allenylic alcohol rac-3r
and subsequent rearomatization afforded all four possible
stereoisomers of differently substituted 3,5-bis-allenylic pyri-
dine 11 with superb diastereo- and enantioselectivity. Overall,
starting from 2a, stereodivergent synthesis of 11 was possible
simply through the choice of the ligand antipode in each step.
Based on the literature reports [52,53] and our prior exper-
imental ﬁndings, [48] a tentative catalytic cycle is depicted in
Scheme 8. Activation of allenylic alcohol ( rac-3) through the
η2-coordination of its terminal double bond to Ir(I)/(P, oleﬁn)
complex (3 → 12) followed by Lewis acid-mediated ionization
of the C─O bond is believed to generate Ir(I)-bound allenylic
carbocation 13.[53] Due to the steric crowding at the si-face
of the η2-Ir(I)-bound planar butadienylium fragment in 13
(R = Ph), caused by the binaphthyl moiety of the axially
bound (Sa)-L on Ir(I), nucleophilic attack of oxazinopyridine
2a is expected to occur at its sterically more accessible re-
face. In this enantiodetermining nucleophilic addition, the
C─C bond formation can take place either from the C3 or
C5 position of 2a, which would give rise to a mixture of
allenylic oxazinopyridines (only 3-allenylic oxazinopyridine
4 is shown here) after deprotonation and decomplexation.
For unsubstituted oxazinopyridine 2a and oxazinopyridine
derived from 4-substituted pyridines, this mixture is inconse-
quential since acid-mediated rearomatization would generate
3-allenylic pyridine ( 5) and 3-allenylic 4-substituted pyridine,
respectively. In the case of 4-methyl oxazinopyridine ( 2v),
1H NMR analysis of the unpuriﬁed intermediate revealed
the incorporation of the allenylic fragment at its dienamine
position (i.e., at C3) (see Supporting Information ). Since
the formation or the absence of the other isomer (i.e., at
C5) could not be conﬁrmed from this NMR analysis, the
possibility of allenylation through the enamine position of
oxazinopyridines cannot be ruled out at this stage. For 3-
substituted pyridines, two regioisomeric oxazinopyridines are
possible. However, each of them contains only one accessible
position for allenylation and upon rearomatization converges
into the same product. In contrast, non-selective nucleophilic
attack of oxazinopyridine derived from 2-substituted pyridine
could generate a regioisomeric mixture of allenylic pyridine
derivatives. However, as shown with 6-aryl oxazinopyridines
2r-u, only 2-aryl 5-allenylic pyridines ( 5ra-ua) were produced
exclusively, arising out of the preferential dienamine reac-
tivity of oxazinopyridines (Scheme 3). Therefore, enantios-
elective synthesis of regioisomeric 2-substituted 3-allenylic
pyridine remains a challenge.
It must be noted that the oxazinopyridines contain two
stereocenters and are used as a mixture of diastereomers in
racemic form. While an inherent substrate bias over stereoin-
duction in the allenylation step gives rise to the likelihood of a
match/mismatch scenario, powerful catalyst control rules out
such a possibility, and meta-allenylic pyridines are obtained
with high e.r. in each case.
Conclusion
In conclusion, we have accomplished enantioselective meta-
allenylation of pyridines via their temporary redox-neutral
dearomatization to easily accessible oxazinopyridines. The
nucleophilic reactivity of oxazinopyridines through their
dienamine-like structural feature was leveraged to achieve

Iridium-Catalyzed Enantioselective Formal meta-Allenylation of
Pyridines
Pankaj Roy+, Pratibha Mahto+, and Santanu Mukherjee*

Abstract: Site-selective functionalization of pyridines is an important yet challenging transformation. Temporary
dearomatization of pyridines through redox-neutral cycloaddition has recently emerged as a reliable and attractive strategy
for meta-functionalization of pyridines. Despite the amenability of the resulting bench-stable cycloadduct, oxazinopyridine,
to a variety of electrophilic and radical-based reagents, its enantioselective functionalization remains unexplored. Herein,
we present the first enantioselective meta-functionalization of pyridines through the intermediacy of oxazinopyridines. This
highly enantioselective formal meta-allenylation of pyridines is achieved by treating the easily accessible oxazinopyridines
with racemic allenylic alcohol under the combination of a catalytic amount of an Ir(I)/(P, olefin) complex and Lewis
acidic Sc(OTf) followed by acid-mediated rearomatization. With oxazinopyridines derived from unsubstituted or suitably
substituted pyridines, iterative 3,5-difunctionalization is possible, which also allows for the stereodivergent synthesis of all
four stereoisomers of 3,5-bis-allenylic pyridines.
Introduction

Pyridine is among the most abundant nitrogenous het-
erocycles in natural products,<sup>[1]</sup> pharmaceuticals,<sup>[2–4]</sup> and
agrochemicals<sup>[5]</sup> (Figure 1). Pyridine derivatives also serve
as ligands<sup>[6]</sup> and catalysts<sup>[7,8]</sup> in asymmetric synthesis besides
acting as precursors to targets of biological and material
importance.<sup>[9]</sup> Consequently, site-selective functionalization
of pyridines is a highly sought-after transformation. Direct
C–H functionalization is the most straightforward avenue
of decorating pyridines.<sup>[10,11]</sup> The inherent electron-deficient
nature of pyridines renders their ortho- and para-positions
electrophilic and amenable to nucleophilic substitution
(Scheme 1a).<sup>[12,13]</sup> In contrast, meta-functionalization of
pyridines is challenging.<sup>[14–16]</sup> Electrophilic aromatic substi-
tution reactions such as nitration<sup>[17]</sup> and bromination<sup>[18]</sup> of
pyridines are known but require harsh reaction conditions,
which restrict their application.

The adversities associated with functionalizing the meta-
position of pyridines have spurred innovative strategies
in recent years.<sup>[14,15]</sup> Various approaches, including
directing group-assisted C–H activation,<sup>[19,20]</sup> non-directed
metalation,<sup>[21–23]</sup> and temporary dearomatization of the
pyridine ring,<sup>[24,25]</sup> have been explored to enable meta-
functionalization, of which the latter emerged as the most
attractive one (Scheme 1b). Among different temporary
dearomatization strategies adopted so far,<sup>[24,26–31]</sup> the redox-

neutral dearomatization of pyridine through cycloaddition is
particularly noteworthy.

In 1967, Huisgen et al. reported a three-component
cycloaddition of pyridine or isoquinoline with dimethyl
acetylenedicarboxylate (DMAD) and phenyl isocyanate,
which could be converted back to its components upon
heating.<sup>[32]</sup> The Nair group further advanced this area by
substituting phenyl isocyanate with other dipolarophiles,
thereby expanding the scope of this reaction.<sup>[33–36]</sup>

Notwithstanding the reversibility of this cycloaddition
reaction, its potential in functionalizing pyridines was not
realized until recently. In 2022, Studer et al. exploited
this strategy to transform pyridines into bench-stable
dearomatized oxazinopyridines C, via Huisgen 1,4-
dipolar cycloaddition with DMAD and methyl pyruvate
(Scheme 1b).<sup>[28]</sup> These oxazinopyridines (oxazinoazines)
are nucleophilic in nature by virtue of their (di)enamine
character and may be viewed as meta-nucleophilic pyridine
surrogates. Consequently, they have been intercepted with a
variety of electrophiles and radical-based reagents prior to
rearomatization to afford meta-substituted pyridines.<sup>[28,37–41]</sup>
In addition, meta-sulfonylation of pyridines has also been
achieved under electrochemical<sup>[42]</sup> or photochemical
conditions.<sup>[43,44]</sup>

Despite their growing popularity, the application of these
meta-nucleophilic pyridine surrogates in catalytic transforma-
tions is rare.<sup>[40,43]</sup> Moreover, this redox-neutral dearomati-
zation strategy has never been applied for enantioselective
functionalization of pyridines or any other azines. In fact,
the only examples of enantioselective meta-functionalization
of pyridines, reported by Wang et al., involve reductive
dearomatization of pyridines.<sup>[45,46]</sup> These processes comprise
of borane-catalyzed dearomative hydroboration of pyridines
to 1,4-dihydropyridines (A, Scheme 1b) followed by Pd-
or Ir-catalyzed enantioselective meta-allylation and oxidative
rearomatization.

In an effort to expand the synthetic toolbox for enan-
tioselective functionalization of pyridines with precise meta-
regioselectivity, we herein report the first enantioselective
functionalization of oxazinopyridines en route to chiral meta-
functionalized pyridines.<sup>[47]</sup>

As a part of our research program on enantioselec-
tive C(sp<sup>2</sup>)–H allenylation under iridium catalysis,<sup>[48,49]</sup> we
became interested in introducing an allenylic substituent at

the meta-position of pyridines. Ir-catalyzed allenylic sub-
stitution reaction was first reported by Takeuchi et al.
in 2004.<sup>[50]</sup> However, Ir-catalyzed enantioselective allenylic
substitution was pioneered by the Carreira group and was
proposed to proceed via an Ir-bound allenylic carbocation
intermediate.<sup>[51–53]</sup> Recent studies by our laboratory<sup>[48]</sup> and
the Takeuchi group<sup>[54]</sup> demonstrated the utility of this catalyst
system for Friedel–Crafts allenylation of (hetero)arenes.
However, electron-deficient nature of pyridines precludes
their direct application in Friedel–Crafts allenylation.

We hypothesized that the nucleophilic (di)enamine func-
tionality of oxazinopyridines<sup>[28]</sup> can be intercepted with an
Ir-bound electrophilic allenylic fragment<sup>[53]</sup> (Scheme 1c).
Subsequent acid-mediated rearomatization would furnish
chiral pyridine derivatives, bearing a synthetically versatile
allenylic group at the meta-position.

steric repulsion with the aryl substituent. To the best of our

Given the prevalence of multifunctional heterocycles in
bioactive molecules,<sup>[2–4]</sup> systematic installation of function-
alities around the pyridine core in a site-selective manner
is an alluring goal. However, such a transformation, espe-
cially involving an enantioselective step, is elusive. Exclusive
C3-selective allenylation of 6-phenyl oxazinopyridine (2r)
intrigued us to assess the possibility of introducing a less
sterically demanding electrophile adjacent to the phenyl
group following enantioselective allenylation. Accordingly,
when 3-allenylic 6-phenyl oxazinopyridine 4ra was subjected
to a reaction with N-chlorosuccinimide (NCS) in CH Cl
at 70 °C,<sup>[28]</sup> chlorination through the enamine functionality
of 4ra indeed took place to yield 5-allenylic-3-chloro-2-
phenylpyridine 10 after rearomatization (Scheme 6).

During the optimization studies (Scheme 2a), bis-
allenylation was encountered with unsubstituted oxazinopy-
ridine 2a. Using 2.2 equiv of rac-3a in this reaction, C -
symmetric 3,5-bis-allenylic pyridine 5aa- was isolated with
excellent relative (>20:1 d.r.) and absolute (>99.5:0.5 e.r.)
stereocontrol (Scheme 7a). The absence of meso-product
indicates complete ligand control in the second allenylation
and opens avenues for stereodivergent<sup>[57]</sup> iterative bis-
allenylation of pyridine with two different allenylic alcohols.

To achieve this goal, controlled mono-allenylation was
performed using an excess of oxazinopyridine 2a for the reac-
tion with 4-fluorophenyl allenylic alcohol rac-3f (Scheme 7b).
Under our otherwise standard reaction conditions, both
stereoisomers of 4af were isolated in good yield. The second
allenylation of 4af with 2-naphthyl allenylic alcohol rac-3r
and subsequent rearomatization afforded all four possible
stereoisomers of differently substituted 3,5-bis-allenylic pyri-

dine 11 with superb diastereo- and enantioselectivity. Overall,
starting from 2a, stereodivergent synthesis of 11 was possible
simply through the choice of the ligand antipode in each step.

Based on the literature reports<sup>[52,53]</sup> and our prior exper-
imental findings,<sup>[48]</sup> a tentative catalytic cycle is depicted in
Scheme 8. Activation of allenylic alcohol (rac-3) through the
η<sup>2</sup>-coordination of its terminal double bond to Ir(I)/(P, olefin)
complex (3 12) followed by Lewis acid-mediated ionization
of the C─O bond is believed to generate Ir(I)-bound allenylic
carbocation 13.<sup>[53]</sup> Due to the steric crowding at the si-face
of the η<sup>2</sup>-Ir(I)-bound planar butadienylium fragment in 13

bound (S )-L on Ir(I), nucleophilic attack of oxazinopyridine
2a is expected to occur at its sterically more accessible re-
face. In this enantiodetermining nucleophilic addition, the
C─C bond formation can take place either from the C3 or
C5 position of 2a, which would give rise to a mixture of
allenylic oxazinopyridines (only 3-allenylic oxazinopyridine
4 is shown here) after deprotonation and decomplexation.
For unsubstituted oxazinopyridine 2a and oxazinopyridine
derived from 4-substituted pyridines, this mixture is inconse-
quential since acid-mediated rearomatization would generate
3-allenylic pyridine (5) and 3-allenylic 4-substituted pyridine,
respectively. In the case of 4-methyl oxazinopyridine (2v),
<sup>1</sup>H NMR analysis of the unpurified intermediate revealed
the incorporation of the allenylic fragment at its dienamine
position (i.e., at C3) (see Supporting Information). Since
the formation or the absence of the other isomer (i.e., at
C5) could not be confirmed from this NMR analysis, the
possibility of allenylation through the enamine position of
oxazinopyridines cannot be ruled out at this stage. For 3-
substituted pyridines, two regioisomeric oxazinopyridines are
possible. However, each of them contains only one accessible
position for allenylation and upon rearomatization converges
into the same product. In contrast, non-selective nucleophilic
attack of oxazinopyridine derived from 2-substituted pyridine
could generate a regioisomeric mixture of allenylic pyridine
derivatives. However, as shown with 6-aryl oxazinopyridines
2r-u, only 2-aryl 5-allenylic pyridines (5ra-ua) were produced
exclusively, arising out of the preferential dienamine reac-
tivity of oxazinopyridines (Scheme 3). Therefore, enantios-
elective synthesis of regioisomeric 2-substituted 3-allenylic
pyridine remains a challenge.

It must be noted that the oxazinopyridines contain two
stereocenters and are used as a mixture of diastereomers in
racemic form. While an inherent substrate bias over stereoin-
duction in the allenylation step gives rise to the likelihood of a
match/mismatch scenario, powerful catalyst control rules out
such a possibility, and meta-allenylic pyridines are obtained
with high e.r. in each case.
Conclusion

In conclusion, we have accomplished enantioselective meta-
allenylation of pyridines via their temporary redox-neutral
dearomatization to easily accessible oxazinopyridines. The
nucleophilic reactivity of oxazinopyridines through their
dienamine-like structural feature was leveraged to achieve
